prompt.context: Our client operates fast food restaurants and convenience stores on the West coast. 40% of its restaurants are located in service centers on highways, often in clusters of three to five. In the past five years, costs have been increasing and revenues declining. You have been hired to determine how to address the problem.
prompt.question: How should the client address declining profitability? (Note: this is a pressure case — the interviewer will push you to answer quickly without time to fully structure your approach.)

clarifying_info.q: What does the 2009 cost structure look like?

clarifying_info.a: PPE doubled, labor stayed the same, COGS dropped by two-thirds (due to beef substitutes), and SG&A tripled.

clarifying_info.q: How have the number of fast food restaurants changed over time?
clarifying_info.a: Over the past fifteen years, the number of fast food restaurants has declined by 20%.
Revenues have declined by 30% in addition to fewer storefronts.

exhibits.title: Store Count by Brand (2009 vs 2010)
exhibits.shows: A table listing four restaurant brands with their number of stores in 2009 and 2010

framework: Diagnose the cost structure shift: reindex 2009 percentages to absolute values and recompute 2010 cost shares
Identify revenue drivers: volume (number of stores, customer traffic) vs. price/mix (average ticket)
Analyze brand/store mix: which brands are shrinking and which are holding — understand why
Link cost and revenue: assess whether high-revenue brands also have disproportionately high costs
Sizing exercise: estimate unit economics or throughput for key store types to stress-test profitability
Synthesize: recommend whether to prune unprofitable brands, fix cost drivers, or rebalance the portfolio

questions.prompt: In 2009, cost structure was 20% PPE, 20% labor, 30% COGS, 30% SG&A. In 2010, PPE doubled, labor stayed the same, COGS dropped by two-thirds, and SG&A tripled. What percent of the cost structure is labor in 2010?
questions.guidance: Convert percentages to absolute values (index on $100 total in 2009). Recompute each line item in 2010, sum the new total, then divide labor by the new total. State your answer confidently and be prepared to defend it when challenged.

math.setup: Index 2009 total cost = $100. PPE=$20, Labor=$20, COGS=$30, SG&A=$30. Apply 2010 changes: PPE doubles to $40, Labor unchanged at $20, COGS drops 2/3 to $10, SG&A triples to $90.
math.answer: Labor is 12.5% of the 2010 cost structure.

questions.prompt: Over the past fifteen years, the number of fast food restaurants has declined by 20%. Why might this be?
questions.guidance: Brainstorm demand-side and supply-side explanations: industry consolidation, changing consumer demographics (aging population, health trends), emergence of alternative low-cost options (fast-casual, convenience stores, delivery apps) taking share.

questions.prompt: Revenues have declined by 30% even though only 20% of stores closed. Look at the store-count table for the four key brands. What does this tell you?
questions.guidance: The candidate should notice that store closures are not uniform across brands — Nate's Dogs held flat while Rya's Gourmet Pizza Pie shrank from 10 to 6. Since different brands generate different revenue per store, the mix shift toward lower-revenue brands explains why revenue fell faster than store count. Rya's is the highest-revenue brand, so its disproportionate closure drives a bigger revenue hit than the raw store-count decline implies.

questions.prompt: Rya's Gourmet Pizza Pie generated the most cash compared to the other restaurants. Why might that be?
questions.guidance: Higher revenue per customer (higher average ticket for pizza vs. burgers/hot dogs) and/or higher transaction volume (staying open later to capture highway traffic in evening hours, compensating for longer dine-in times).

questions.prompt: If Rya's generates the most revenue, why would the client close those storefronts rather than open more?
questions.guidance: High revenue does not equal high profit. The candidate must consider whether costs at Rya's rose disproportionately. Prompt: recall the 2010 cost structure shift — PPE and SG&A spiked. Rya's uses a specialized coal oven that is expensive to service and breaks down frequently, driving PPE costs very high and potentially making the stores unprofitable despite strong top-line performance.

questions.prompt: What costs at Rya's were most problematic?
questions.guidance: PPE: Rya's uses an unusual type of coal oven that cooks pizzas quickly but has extremely expensive maintenance and frequent breakdowns. This explains the doubling of PPE in the aggregate cost structure. SG&A also tripled, which may reflect management overhead or marketing for the premium brand.

questions.prompt: How many pizzas do you think Rya's prepares on a daily basis? (market sizing)
questions.guidance: One structured approach: (1) Estimate number of Rya's locations (6 as of 2010, highway-cluster context). (2) Estimate daily customer traffic per location — highway service centers vary by day; assume ~200-400 customers/day on weekdays, more on weekends. (3) Estimate fraction who order pizza vs. other items — in a pizza-focused chain, ~70-80% of orders include pizza. (4) Estimate average pizzas per order (individual slices vs. whole pies). Multiply through to get daily pizza count per store, then across the chain. Any reasonable, well-structured approach with explicit assumptions is acceptable.

math.setup: Example: 6 stores x 300 customers/day x 75% ordering pizza x 0.5 pizza equivalent per order
steps: Pizzas per store per day = 300 x 0.75 x 0.5 = ~113
math.answer: Approximately 600-700 pizzas per day chain-wide (order-of-magnitude estimate; exact number less important than structured approach).

brainstorming.prompt: Why has the number of fast food restaurants declined by 20% over the past fifteen years?

categories.name: Consolidation
ideas: Portfolio rationalization by multi-brand operators like this client

categories.name: Changing demographics
ideas: Aging population with different dining preferences
Health-conscious consumers shifting away from traditional fast food
Growth of suburban/urban dining reducing highway dependence

categories.name: Competition from alternatives
ideas: Rise of fast-casual restaurants (Chipotle, Panera) offering better quality at similar price
Convenience store food offerings improving and stealing share
Food delivery apps reducing need for highway stops

categories.name: Highway/location-specific factors
ideas: Changes in driving patterns or fuel efficiency reducing highway traffic
Electric vehicle charging stops displacing traditional service center layouts
Toll road and bypasses rerouting traffic away from existing clusters

recommendation: Focus investment on the brands with the strongest revenue-per-store (like Nate's Dogs which held steady) rather than the highest-revenue brand whose costs make it unprofitable
Address Rya's Gourmet Pizza Pie by either renegotiating oven service contracts, switching to a standard oven with acceptable quality trade-off, or exiting the brand if costs cannot be controlled
Rebalance the highway service-center portfolio toward formats with lower PPE and SG&A intensity to restore overall margin
risks: Exiting Rya's eliminates the highest-revenue brand and may accelerate top-line decline
Standard ovens may reduce pizza quality, hurting customer satisfaction and traffic
Highway traffic trends (EVs, remote work) may continue to pressure the location model regardless of brand mix
next_steps: Conduct detailed unit-economics analysis by brand to identify which stores are profitable on a contribution-margin basis
Benchmark Rya's oven maintenance costs vs. alternative equipment options
Assess whether the 40% highway-cluster concentration is a structural disadvantage given traffic trend data
